newsitem.title: USA: Perry faces hostile Republicans on Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Perry faces hostile Republicans on Bosnia.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Perry told Congress on Thursday that President Bill Clinton was not misleading Americans on Bosnia, saying Clinton had made no decision yet on sending U.S. troops there next year.

To scathing criticism from Republicans, Perry denied that 5,000 U.S. troops who will begin entering Bosnia within days to cover the removal of 15,800 American soldiers there are the planned vanguard for a new international force in Bosnia.

But he also told the Senate Armed Services Committee that "the international interest in Bosnia has not ended," and left open the possibility that U.S. forces could be part of a possible new NATO-led peacekeeping force in 1997.

"I can assure you I have made no recommendation to the president on a follow-on force. He has made no decision on a follow-on force at this time," Perry testified, adding that NATO was currently studing such a new force for Bosnia.

The current NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR) of 52,000 in shattered Bosnia is scheduled to leave in December. No decision has been made, but many allies are calling for a follow-on force and pressing hard for U.S. participation.

"Gentlemen, the credibility gap between you and the Congress is as wide as the Grand Canyon," Republican Sen. John McCain of Arizona told Perry and Army General John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

With Clinton facing a reelection vote against challenger Bob Dole on November 5, McCain and other Republicans slammed the plan to send in the cover force, especially after Shalikashvili said that some of those troops would remain until mid-March.

McCain and others accused Clinton of violating a promise to remove U.S. forces from Bosnia by this December 20 under the Dayton peace accord and questioned whether the new troops were a virtual commitment by Washington to go back to Bosnia.

"The fact that we still have no (Bosnia) exit strategy is still foreboding for the United States," added Republican Sen. Dirk Kempthorne of Idaho. He compared Bosnia to the long, bitter U.S. military experience in Vietnam.
The December 20 pull-out date has already slipped weeks into early 1997 because an adequate NATO-led force is being kept longer to help keep peace during municipal elections in November.
Republicans have demanded that Congress have a final say on whether U.S. forces are again committed to Bosnia.
Democrat Clinton leads Republican challenger Dole comfortably in current polls, but surveys also show that many Americans would oppose returning Americans troops to Bosnia in any new force next year.
Perry stressed that while he had made no decision on a recommendation to Clinton, he was seriously considering three "viable" options for the United States in Bosnia:
-- Complete and final removal of the current force and no further participation.
-- Preventing war from breaking out again by using warplanes and international troops on stand-by outside of Bosnia.
-- Sending a "stabilization" force into Bosnia to maintain a safe atmosphere for civilians and help improve conditions for a lasting peace between Serbs, Muslins and Croats.
But Republicans charged that Perry and other administration officials repeatedly assured Congress last December that a year in Bosnia would be enough for the success of IFOR.
Virginia Sen. John Warner noted that former U.S. peace negotiator to Bosnia Richard Holbrooke told the committee last December 7:
"We think a year is sufficient. If a year does not work, two, three or five years will not do it either."

Holbrooke and retired U.S. Navy Admiral Leighton Smith, who headed IFOR until this summer, told Congress eariler this week that continued peace in Bosnia would require a new military peacekeeping force next year.
